newsitem.title: UK: Summary of latest opinion polls on EMU.
newsitem.headline: Summary of latest opinion polls on EMU.

text.p: The following is a summary of findings from recent independent opinion polls and surveys about European economic and monetary union (EMU).
SWEDEN, June 18 - The number of Swedish market players that expect EMU to start on time was 81 percent in June, pollster Temo said. This compares with 82 percent in May.

EUROPE, June 17 - A telephone survey of around 6,000 people in seven EU countries published in Brussels by French bank Sofinco showed that 43 percent thought the introduction of the euro would be more inconvenient than beneficial. Another 25 percent either didn't know or couldn't say, while 32 percent were in favour.

GERMANY, June 14 - A slim majority of Germans is against the planned single European currency with the strongest opposition coming from eastern Germany and left-leaning voters, a survey by the Forsa institute found. The survey of 1,011 Germans found that 51 percent opposed the euro's introduction while 34 percent were in favour.

EUROPE, June 13 - Expectations that Italy will join core European countries in founding EMU in 1999 edged up in a week in which France turned the spotlight on job creation and growth, prices monitored by JP Morgan showed. Though the perceived likelihood of Spain and Portugal joining their ranks drifted down, hopes of the U.K. and Ireland joining EMU from the outset took the biggest battering, according to the JP Morgan "EMU calculator", derived primarily from the interest-rate swaps market.

The probability of Irish membership tumbled to 41 percent from 54 percent last week and 63 percent in mid-May, while the implied likelihood of the U.K. joining slumped to 38 percent from 45 percent a week ago and a post-election high of 53 percent at the end of May.

GERMANY, June 12 - Almost half the German population is fearful of Europe's planned single currency because of worries the euro will be worth less than their German mark, an opinion survey conducted by the Wickert Institute said.
The poll said 47 percent of 870 adults surveyed were frightened by the proposed single currency while 53 percent said they were not concerned.

GERMANY, June 12 - Europe's single currency may be unpopular in Germany but it will not become a campaign issue next year because the pro and contra camps are not clearly defined along party lines, according to a leading pollster.

Elisabeth Noelle-Neumann, head of the Allenbach Institute and doyenne of German opinion researchers, said her surveys showed 52 percent of Germans were against the euro and this would not change much before the September 1998 election.

GERMANY, June 12 - Fifty-four percent of Germans surveyed in the Allensbach Institute's latest monthly poll said they expected EMU to start on time even though 52 percent said they were against it. Only 22 percent said they supported the single currency.

FRANCE, June 11 - A majority of French people think the new Socialist-led government should continue talks with its European partners to find new conditions for joining a single currency rather than doing everything possible to hit the Maastricht treaty criteria, according to a CSA poll.

Fifty-eight percent of 1,000 French people polled on June 9 said they believed France should continue talks, rather than impose new austerity to hit the strict three percent deficit target, even if this risked compromising the move to a single European currency. Twenty-seven percent of those polled said France should do everything possible to hit the deficit target.

DENMARK, June 9 - Danish resistance to EMU has changed little over the past three months, an opinion poll published in the financial daily Borsen said.The survey, by Greens polling institute, showed 55.9 percent of respondents saying that Denmark should stick to its existing policy of staying out of monetary union, compared to 55.6 percent in a March poll.

The latest survey, of 1,015 respondents over the period from June 2 to June 4, showed 32.5 percent in favour of EMU compared to 33.4 percent in March, while the number of don't knows grew to 11.6 percent in the new poll from 10.9 percent.

GERMANY, June 8 - Eighty-two percent of Germans, parting company with Chancellor Helmut Kohl, want EMU to be delayed if member countries cannot meet the Maastricht criteria, according to an IRNA poll for Focus magazine. The respondents were evenly split on whether the single currency would be launched on time.

EUROPE, June 6 - Expectations of a broad-based start to EMU were little changed even as developments in France and Germany increased perceptions of a wider, softer euro, prices monitored by JP Morgan showed Friday.

The perceived EMU probability in Sweden -- which announced it would not join EMU from the start -- drifted slightly lower to 61 percent while Spain's chances as assumed by markets firmed a touch to 77 percent from 75 last week.

The JP Morgan "EMU" calculator showed the probability of France and Germany founding the single currency unchanged at 100 percent. The implied probability of Belgium joining EMU from the start returned to 100 percent from 96 last week.
Overall, expectations that other EMU hopefuls will join Germany and France from the start were little changed.

GERMANY, June 6 - A slender majority of Germans are opposed to Bonn's plan to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves to help Germany qualify for EMU, according to a survey, carried out by the DIMAP research institute for the newspaper Bild and the MDR television channel. The poll found that 52 percent of the 1,100 Germans interviewed were against the plan, while 37 percent were in favour. Eleven percent had no opinion.
FINLAND, June 5 - Forty-four percent of Finns oppose joining EMU against 36 percent in favour, according to Finnish news agency STT, citing a new poll by research company Taloustutkimus.
It did not make clear if the remaining 20 percent in the poll, for the Conservative Party's Verkkouutiset paper, were undecided.

FRANCE, June 5 - A majority of voters want France to renegotiate conditions for joining the single European currency, according to an Ipsos poll on Thursday, the first such survey since a left-wing victory in a parliamentary election.
The survey, to be published in the weekly Le Point, said a 52 to 36 percent majority favoured renegotiating the Maastricht treaty conditions for qualifying for the euro from 1999.
